changedBeliefs: The `parameter-encoding-and-binding` open question — does exp 234's `TransferableTypedData` blob-transfer win extend to the batch (`BatchRequest`/`executeBatch`) path carrying per-set blobs — is answered NO. On a blob-heavy `executeBatch` (30 rows/batch, one blob param each), wrapping each qualifying blob is a reproduced REGRESSION at the sizes where single-row INSERT won: 256 KB is candidate-slower on 8/8 order-flipped legs across four runs (+7.6% to +18.1%, median ~+9.5%), 512 KB leans slower (7/8 legs), and 1 MB is uniformly slightly slower (WAL-dominated). No payload size shows a win. Sub-threshold 64/128 KB same-code-path controls swing +/-100%+ in both directions, which calibrates the noise floor — the wrapped-lane regression reproduces same-direction where the controls' noise does not.

The exp 234 blob-transfer win is NOT 'large blobs on the GC heap are expensive' in the abstract; it is specific to MANY INDEPENDENT WRITE ROUND-TRIPS. The mechanism: across N single-row INSERTs, each `SendPort.send` parks a fresh blob on the young-generation heap, and a scavenge triggered while the writer is mid-`sqlite3_step` on the *previous* blob safepoints the whole isolate group including the writer — a stall that compounds over N round-trips and that moving blobs into GC-invisible malloc'd memory removes. `executeBatch` carries all N parameter sets across ONE `SendPort.send` and runs them in ONE writer round-trip inside one transaction, so there is no interleaving of scavenge-versus-writer-step to reclaim. The very cost exp 234 optimized is absent in the batch path.

With the reclaimable cost gone, wrapping a batch is pure tax: the candidate pays 30x `TransferableTypedData.fromList` (malloc + finalizer + external-memory accounting that itself pressures the GC) plus 30x `materialize()`, against a baseline whose single object-graph copy of all 30 blobs is a one-time transient the writer never races. This bounds exp 234: batching is a form of round-trip coalescing (like exp 180), and coalescing removes exactly the churn the wrap reclaims. Any transport optimization justified by per-round-trip GC/safepoint interaction should be re-checked, not assumed, once the round-trips are collapsed.
nextSignals: Batch blob transfer is closed under the many-mid-size-blob shape. Reopen only under: (a) a Dart runtime change that makes `TransferableTypedData` wrapping cheap enough that the per-blob tax disappears (then a small batch benefit could surface), or (b) a production workload showing a SINGLE `executeBatch` carrying one or few VERY LARGE blobs, where per-blob wrap cost amortizes over fewer sets and the batch's own WAL cost is large — a materially different shape from the 30x mid-size batch tested here. Do not retry the many-mid-size shape without new runtime evidence.

`benchmark/experiments/blob_batch_write_ab.dart` is the durable gate for any batch-blob-transfer revisit (30 rows/batch, 64 KB-1 MB, runtime-toggled threshold, order-flipped). The runtime prototype (`wrapBlobParamSets`/`unwrapBlobParamSets` + `BatchRequest`/`_handleBatch` wiring) is preserved at `archive/exp-237` for cherry-pick.

Generalizable methodology note: exp 234's own signal predicted this would 'reproduce the same transfer fraction'; it did not, because the batch changes the round-trip count, not just the blob-size total. A blob-transfer win measured on single-row writes does not transfer to a coalesced/batched path by blob-size similarity — the round-trip topology is the load-bearing variable.

claims.text: Exp 234's blob-transfer win does not extend to executeBatch: wrapping per-set blobs is a reproduced regression. The mechanism is many independent write round-trips parking fresh blobs on the young heap — one batch round-trip does not have it.
